title: Haptic glove force-feedback density
bottleneck: Realistic touch needs per-finger force feedback that can resist motion (kinesthetic) plus skin-level texture (tactile), but actuators small enough for gloves are weak, bulky, power-hungry, or slow. Current gloves do vibration or limited force on a few fingers; full-hand, high-fidelity force feedback remains a lab exoskeleton. Heat and battery add more bulk.
why_it_blocks: Without convincing hand haptics, virtual objects feel like ghosts: you see your hand pass through what your eyes say is solid. The hand is where the reality gap is most keenly felt.
current_state: Commercial haptic gloves offer vibrotactile feedback with limited force; research exoskeletons demonstrate strong force feedback at the cost of wearability. No glove combines fidelity, comfort, and affordability. Actuators strong enough to resist a finger are too large to fit ten of them in a glove, forcing a choice between coverage and strength.
